title: Table Saw
description: The table saw is the workshop's central ripping and crosscutting machine: a circular blade rises through a flat table, and the workpiece is guided past it by a rip fence or a miter gauge. A standard 10-inch blade at about 4,800 revolutions per minute gives a fast, clean cut in sheet goods and solid lumber, and the fence must be parallel to the blade or the cut will bind. This guide covers a first safe practice project, a simple pine shelf board ripped to width and crosscut to length, with the blade guard and riving knife in place throughout. Never reach over a spinning blade, never cut freehand without fence or gauge, and always use a push stick when the fence is within six inches of the blade.

image.description: Original diagram for Table Saw: Pine shelf board, ripped to width and crosscut to length. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.

specs.dimensions: 10-inch blade, 3 horsepower motor, rip capacity 30 inches to the right of the blade, maximum cut depth 3-1/8 inches at 90 degrees
details: Blade tip speed: about 12,566 ft/min at 4,800 rpm
Maximum depth of cut: 3.125 in at 90 degrees, 2.25 in at 45 degrees
fasteners: No fasteners in the practice cut; the shelf is joined later with screws
specs.tolerances: Rip width within 1/32 inch of target; squareness within 1/64 inch over 12 inches
specs.arithmetic_note: Tip speed checks out: circumference pi x diameter times rpm, divided by 12 inches per foot. Demo output below was captured by executing the demo code at build time.

steps: Unplug the saw, fit the 40-tooth blade, and set the riving knife and guard in place.
Set the blade height so the highest tooth sits about 1/8 inch above the board surface.
Set the rip fence to the shelf width and check it parallel to the blade with a square.
With eye and hearing protection on, start the saw, wait for full speed, and feed the pine board steadily with a push stick past the blade.
Crosscut the ripped board to length with the miter gauge, keeping hands clear of the blade path.
Switch off, wait for the blade to stop completely, then measure the finished shelf board.

required: Table Saw (the tool of this guide)
Push stick or featherboard where applicable
tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection and hearing protection. Keep hands clear of the blade or cutter path, keep guards in place, use a push stick or featherboard where fitted, disconnect power before changing a blade or bit, and never defeat a guard or reach over a spinning blade.

demo.code:
import math
D=10
RPM=4800
circ=math.pi*D
ftmin=circ*RPM/12.0
print('Blade diameter: ' + str(D) + ' in, speed: ' + str(RPM) + ' rpm')
print('Circumference: %.2f in' % circ)
print('Blade tip speed: %.0f ft/min' % ftmin)
print('Tip speed: %.1f mph' % (ftmin*60/5280.0))
demo.expected_output:
Blade diameter: 10 in, speed: 4800 rpm
Circumference: 31.42 in
Blade tip speed: 12566 ft/min
Tip speed: 142.8 mph

title: Miter Saw
description: The miter saw makes accurate crosscuts and angled cuts: the blade head pivots down onto a workpiece held against a fence, and the head can swing left and right for miters and tilt for bevels. A 12-inch sliding miter saw cuts boards up to about 14 inches wide, and its detents lock at common angles such as 45 and 90 degrees. This guide covers cutting picture-frame miters at 45 degrees, a forgiving first project that teaches angle setup, clamping, and measuring. Keep hands at least six inches from the blade path, let the blade reach full speed before lowering it, and let it stop before raising the head.

image.description: Original diagram for Miter Saw: Poplar picture frame with 45-degree mitered corners. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.

Cut the matching 45-degree piece and test-fit the corner before gluing.
Glue and brad the frame, then check both diagonals are equal.

title: Circular Saw
description: The circular saw is a portable 7-1/4-inch saw that brings the cut to the workpiece, and with a straightedge guide it breaks down full plywood sheets accurately. Its base plate rides on the sheet while the blade cuts from below, so the good face goes down to keep tear-out on the hidden side. This guide covers breaking down a plywood sheet into shelf panels with a clamped straightedge, the single most useful circular-saw skill. The blade guard must snap back after every cut, the cord must stay behind the saw, and the sheet must be fully supported so the offcut cannot pinch the blade.

image.description: Original diagram for Circular Saw: Plywood shelf panels cut from a full sheet. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.

specs.dimensions: 7-1/4-inch blade, 15 amp motor, maximum cut depth 2-7/16 inches at 90 degrees, bevel capacity 57 degrees
details: Blade: 7.25 in diameter, 24-tooth framing blade (40-tooth for plywood)
Blade tip speed: about 11,005 ft/min at 5,800 rpm
fasteners: Shelf panels joined later with 1-1/4 inch screws
specs.tolerances: Guided cut straight within 1/32 inch over 48 inches; panel width within 1/16 inch
specs.arithmetic_note: Tip speed checks out: circumference pi x diameter times rpm, divided by 12 inches per foot. Demo output below was captured by executing the demo code at build time.

steps: Support the plywood sheet on sawhorses so the cut line hangs free and the offcut cannot pinch.
Measure the distance from blade to base-plate edge and clamp the straightedge that far from the cut line.
Set the blade depth to about 1/4 inch below the sheet.
With the good face down, start the saw clear of the sheet, reach full speed, and push steadily along the guide.
Let the blade stop before setting the saw down, then check the panel width.
Repeat for each shelf panel, re-clamping the guide for every cut.

required: Circular Saw (the tool of this guide)
Push stick or featherboard where applicable
tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection and hearing protection. Keep hands clear of the blade or cutter path, keep guards in place, use a push stick or featherboard where fitted, disconnect power before changing a blade or bit, and never defeat a guard or reach over a spinning blade.

title: Jigsaw
description: The jigsaw cuts curves and interior openings with a thin reciprocating blade, and it is the safest powered saw to learn on because the blade is small and the cut is slow and visible. Blade choice decides the result: fine-tooth blades for clean curves in thin stock, coarse blades for fast rough cuts. This guide covers cutting a rounded-corner shelf bracket from pine, including drilling a starter hole for an interior cut. Keep the shoe flat on the work, let the blade do the cutting rather than forcing it, and never put fingers under the workpiece near the blade.

image.description: Original diagram for Jigsaw: Rounded-corner pine shelf bracket. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="400" height="220" viewBox="0 0 400 220"><title>Jigsaw tool diagram</title><rect x="20" y="140" width="360" height="18" fill="#8a6d3b"/><circle cx="200" cy="110" r="62" fill="none" stroke="hsl(92,40%,40%)" stroke-width="6"/><circle cx="200" cy="110" r="10" fill="hsl(92,40%,40%)"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="258" y2="110" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="228" y2="160" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="171" y2="160" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="143" y2="110" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="172" y2="60" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="229" y2="60" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="290" y="120" width="70" height="20" fill="#555"/><text x="200" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Jigsaw</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Variable-speed motor, orbital action settings 0 to 3, maximum cut depth 3-3/8 inches in wood, stroke length 1 inch
details: Blade: T-shank, 10 teeth per inch for curves in 3/4 in stock
Speed: variable, up to about 3,000 strokes per minute
fasteners: Bracket mounted later with 1-1/2 inch screws
specs.tolerances: Curve within 1/16 inch of the marked line; bracket corners matched as a pair
specs.arithmetic_note: Grit sequence checks out: every step is coarser-to-finer in strictly ascending order. Demo output below was captured by executing the demo code at build time.

steps: Mark the rounded corner on the pine blank and clamp it to the bench with the curve overhanging.
Fit a 10-teeth-per-inch curve blade and set the orbital action to 1 for a clean cut.
Start the saw clear of the work, reach speed, and guide the blade along the line without pushing sideways.
Slow down on tight curves and back out of the cut if the blade binds.
Sand the sawn edge through 120-grit, then 180-grit, and check the bracket against its pair.
Test-fit the bracket under a shelf before mounting.

required: Push stick or featherboard where applicable
tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection and hearing protection. Keep hands clear of the blade or cutter path, keep guards in place, use a push stick or featherboard where fitted, disconnect power before changing a blade or bit, and never defeat a guard or reach over a spinning blade.

demo.code:
SEQ=[80, 120, 180]
print('Grit progression: ' + ', '.join(str(x) for x in SEQ))
asc=all(SEQ[i]<SEQ[i+1] for i in range(len(SEQ)-1))
print('Steps: ' + str(len(SEQ)))
print('Strictly ascending: ' + str(asc))
print('First grit: ' + str(SEQ[0]) + ', last grit: ' + str(SEQ[-1]))
demo.expected_output:
Grit progression: 80, 120, 180
Steps: 3
Strictly ascending: True
First grit: 80, last grit: 180

title: Band Saw
description: The band saw runs a continuous loop blade around two wheels, and it is the right machine for resawing boards into thinner pieces and for cutting tight curves that a jigsaw cannot follow cleanly. Blade width sets the minimum curve radius: a 1/4-inch blade turns a radius of about 5/8 inch, while a 1/2-inch blade suits straight resawing. This guide covers resawing a pine board into two book-matched panels, the classic band-saw practice piece. The blade guard must sit just above the work, hands must never cross the blade line, and the work must be fed with the fence or a featherboard, never freehand against a tall fence.

image.description: Original diagram for Band Saw: Book-matched pine panels resawn from one board. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.

specs.dimensions: 14-inch wheels, 1 horsepower motor, resaw capacity 6 inches (with riser block 12 inches), table tilts 0 to 45 degrees
details: Blade: 1/2 in wide, 3 teeth per inch hook tooth for resawing
Resaw capacity: 6 in standard, 12 in with riser block
Minimum curve radius for 1/4 in blade: about 0.625 in
fasteners: Book-matched panels joined later with glue only
specs.tolerances: Resawn panels within 1/32 inch thickness of each other; cut face flat within 1/64 inch
specs.arithmetic_note: Kerf waste checks out: cut count times kerf width, subtracted from the starting length. Demo output below was captured by executing the demo code at build time.

steps: Fit the 1/2-inch, 3-teeth-per-inch blade and tension it per the saw's gauge.
Set the blade guard just above the pine blank and square the fence to the blade.
Mark the resaw line around the blank and start the saw.
Feed steadily against the fence with a push stick, keeping hands clear of the blade line.
Plane or sand the sawn faces lightly, then open the two panels like a book to check the match.
Measure both panels and keep the pair together for the project.

required: Band Saw (the tool of this guide)
Push stick or featherboard where applicable
tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection and hearing protection. Keep hands clear of the blade or cutter path, keep guards in place, use a push stick or featherboard where fitted, disconnect power before changing a blade or bit, and never defeat a guard or reach over a spinning blade.

demo.code:
CUTS=1
KERF=0.042
LEN=48
waste=CUTS*KERF
rem=LEN-waste
print('Cuts: ' + str(CUTS) + ', kerf: ' + str(KERF) + ' in')
print('Kerf waste total: %.3f in' % waste)
print('Board length: ' + str(LEN) + ' in, length left after kerf loss: %.3f in' % rem)

Kerf waste total: 0.042 in
Board length: 48 in, length left after kerf loss: 47.958 in

title: Router
description: The router spins a shaped bit at 20,000 revolutions per minute or more and cuts profiles, grooves, dados, and edge treatments that no saw can make. Direction matters: feeding against the bit's rotation gives control, while feeding with the rotation (climb cutting) can snatch the workpiece. This guide covers routing a round-over edge on a pine shelf, the most common first router job, using a bearing-guided bit that follows the edge. The bit must be seated fully in the collet, the workpiece must be clamped, and the router must be switched off and still before it is set down.

image.description: Original diagram for Router: Round-over edge on a pine shelf. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="400" height="220" viewBox="0 0 400 220"><title>Router tool diagram</title><rect x="20" y="140" width="360" height="18" fill="#8a6d3b"/><circle cx="200" cy="110" r="62" fill="none" stroke="hsl(148,40%,40%)" stroke-width="6"/><circle cx="200" cy="110" r="10" fill="hsl(148,40%,40%)"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="258" y2="110" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="228" y2="160" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="171" y2="160" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="143" y2="110" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="172" y2="60" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="229" y2="60" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="290" y="120" width="70" height="20" fill="#555"/><text x="200" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Router</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: 2-1/4 horsepower motor, variable speed 10,000 to 25,000 rpm, collet sizes 1/4 inch and 1/2 inch, plunge depth 2-1/2 inches
details: Bit: 1/4 in radius round-over, 1/2 in shank, bearing-guided
Speed for 1 in diameter bit: about 18,000 rpm
Pass depth for edge profile: full profile in one pass on 3/4 in stock
Feed rate: about 60 in per minute for softwood edge work
specs.tolerances: Round-over profile even along the full edge; no burn marks deeper than surface discoloration
specs.arithmetic_note: Feed time checks out: cut length divided by the feed rate in inches per minute. Demo output below was captured by executing the demo code at build time.

steps: Fit the 1/4-inch round-over bit with at least 3/4 inch of shank in the collet and tighten firmly.
Set the bearing to ride on the shelf edge and test the depth on an offcut.
Clamp the pine shelf to the bench and put on eye and hearing protection.
Start the router clear of the work, reach full speed, and feed against the bit rotation along the edge.
Make a second light pass if any burn marks appear, then sand the edge with 180-grit.
Check the profile by running a fingertip along the full edge.

required: Push stick or featherboard where applicable
tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection and hearing protection. Keep hands clear of the blade or cutter path, keep guards in place, use a push stick or featherboard where fitted, disconnect power before changing a blade or bit, and never defeat a guard or reach over a spinning blade.

demo.code:
IPM=60
LEN=48
mins=LEN/IPM
print('Feed rate: ' + str(IPM) + ' in per minute, cut length: ' + str(LEN) + ' in')
print('Cut time: %.2f minutes' % mins)
print('Cut time: %.0f seconds' % (mins*60))

Cut time: 0.80 minutes

title: Planer
description: The thickness planer shaves the top face of a board to a uniform thickness, turning rough lumber into flat, even stock. It removes only a small amount per pass, about 1/16 inch in hardwood and 1/8 inch in softwood, and it must never be used on a board shorter than the manufacturer's minimum length, because short boards can kick back. This guide covers planing a rough pine board down to a clean 3/4-inch thickness for a shelf. Always plane with the grain, support long boards at both ends, and never reach into the machine while the cutterhead is spinning.

image.description: Original diagram for Planer: Rough pine board planed to a clean 3/4-inch shelf board. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="400" height="220" viewBox="0 0 400 220"><title>Planer tool diagram</title><rect x="20" y="140" width="360" height="18" fill="#8a6d3b"/><circle cx="200" cy="110" r="62" fill="none" stroke="hsl(56,40%,40%)" stroke-width="6"/><circle cx="200" cy="110" r="10" fill="hsl(56,40%,40%)"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="258" y2="110" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="228" y2="160" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="171" y2="160" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="143" y2="110" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="172" y2="60" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="229" y2="60" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="290" y="120" width="70" height="20" fill="#555"/><text x="200" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Planer</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: 13-inch width capacity, 6-inch maximum board thickness, two-knife cutterhead at about 10,000 rpm, feed rate about 26 feet per minute
details: Maximum cut per pass: 0.0625 in hardwood, 0.125 in softwood
Target thickness: 0.75 in from 1 in rough (4 passes at 1/16 in)
fasteners: No fasteners; planed board joined later
specs.tolerances: Final thickness within 0.010 inch across the board; no snipe deeper than 0.010 inch at the ends
specs.arithmetic_note: Board feet check out: thickness x width x length in inches divided by 144, times the board count. Demo output below was captured by executing the demo code at build time.

steps: Measure the rough board and mark the target 3/4-inch thickness.
Set the planer to remove 1/16 inch and feed the board with the grain, supported at both ends.
Flip the board end for end between passes to keep the cut even.
Measure thickness after each pass and stop at 3/4 inch.
Sand the planed faces lightly with 150-grit to remove cutter marks.
Check the board for flatness with a straightedge before use.

required: Push stick or featherboard where applicable
tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection and hearing protection. Keep hands clear of the blade or cutter path, keep guards in place, use a push stick or featherboard where fitted, disconnect power before changing a blade or bit, and never defeat a guard or reach over a spinning blade.

demo.code:
T=0.75
W=8
L=48
N=4
PRICE=3.5
bf=T*W*L/144.0
tot=bf*N
print('Board: ' + str(T) + ' in thick x ' + str(W) + ' in wide x ' + str(L) + ' in long')
print('Board feet per board: %.2f' % bf)
print('Boards: ' + str(N) + ', total board feet: %.2f' % tot)
print('Cost at $%.2f per board foot: $%.2f' % (PRICE, tot*PRICE))
demo.expected_output:
Board: 0.75 in thick x 8 in wide x 48 in long
Board feet per board: 2.00
Boards: 4, total board feet: 8.00
Cost at $3.50 per board foot: $28.00

title: Jointer
description: The jointer flattens one face and squares one edge of a board, which is the first step before the planer can make the opposite face parallel. It is an advanced machine because the cutterhead is exposed between the infeed and outfeed tables, and hands must always ride on the outfeed side once the cut starts. This guide covers jointing one face and one edge of a twisted pine board until it sits flat without rocking. Use push blocks, never bare hands over the cutterhead, and never joint stock shorter than 12 inches or thinner than 1/2 inch.

image.description: Original diagram for Jointer: Twisted pine board flattened on one face and squared on one edge. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.

Joint one edge against the 90-degree fence until it is straight and square to the face.
Mark the jointed face and edge as reference faces for the planer.

title: Drill Press
description: The drill press drills straight, repeatable holes at a set depth, which a hand drill cannot guarantee. Speed is set by belt position: large bits run slow, small bits run fast, and Forstner bits need a slow speed and firm clamping. This guide covers drilling clean 1-inch shelf-pin holes in a pine side panel with a Forstner bit and a depth stop. Clamp the work every time, never hold small pieces by hand near the bit, and switch off before clearing chips.

image.description: Original diagram for Drill Press: Shelf-pin holes drilled in a pine side panel. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.

Hole depth: 0.375 in for shelf pins
fasteners: Shelf pins: 1/4 inch diameter metal pins, 4 per shelf
specs.tolerances: Hole depth within 1/64 inch; hole spacing within 1/32 inch; holes perpendicular within 1 degree

Fit the 1-inch Forstner bit, set the speed to the slowest belt position, and set the depth stop to 3/8 inch.

Lower the bit steadily, clear chips by raising the bit, and drill to the depth stop.
Repeat for each hole, re-clamping if the panel moves.
Test-fit shelf pins in every hole before assembly.

Push stick or featherboard where applicable
tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection and hearing protection. Keep hands clear of the blade or cutter path, keep guards in place, use a push stick or featherboard where fitted, disconnect power before changing a blade or bit, and never defeat a guard or reach over a spinning blade.

title: Orbital Sander
description: The random orbital sander smooths surfaces without the swirl marks a belt sander leaves, because its pad both spins and orbits. Grit progression is the whole skill: start at 80 or 100 grit to remove saw marks, then 150, then 220 for a finish-ready surface, and never skip more than one grit step. This guide covers sanding a pine shelf board finish-ready, including dust extraction and a final hand-sanding pass with the grain. Wear a dust mask, connect extraction where available, and never press hard, because pressure slows the pad and causes swirls.

image.description: Original diagram for Orbital Sander: Pine shelf board sanded finish-ready. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="400" height="220" viewBox="0 0 400 220"><title>Orbital Sander tool diagram</title><rect x="20" y="140" width="360" height="18" fill="#8a6d3b"/><circle cx="200" cy="110" r="62" fill="none" stroke="hsl(151,40%,40%)" stroke-width="6"/><circle cx="200" cy="110" r="10" fill="hsl(151,40%,40%)"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="258" y2="110" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="228" y2="160" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="171" y2="160" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="143" y2="110" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="172" y2="60" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="110" x2="229" y2="60" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="290" y="120" width="70" height="20" fill="#555"/><text x="200" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Orbital Sander</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: 5-inch pad, 12,000 orbits per minute, 3/16-inch orbit diameter, hook-and-loop discs
details: Orbit: 0.1875 in diameter, about 12,000 orbits per minute
Dust port: fits standard shop vacuum hose
Sanding rate: about 4 sq ft per minute at 150 grit on pine
specs.tolerances: Surface smooth to the touch with no visible scratches at 220 grit; no sand-through on edges
specs.arithmetic_note: Grit sequence checks out: every step is coarser-to-finer in strictly ascending order. Demo output below was captured by executing the demo code at build time.

steps: Fit a 100-grit disc and sand the pine board with light pressure, moving steadily with the grain.
Vacuum the dust and switch to 150-grit, sanding the full surface again.
Vacuum again and finish with 220-grit, then hand-sand lightly with 220-grit along the grain.
Wipe the surface with a tack cloth and inspect in raking light for scratches.
Repeat any scratched area from the previous grit, not just the last one.
The board is finish-ready when it feels uniformly smooth.

required: Orbital Sander (the tool of this guide)
Push stick or featherboard where applicable
tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection and hearing protection. Keep hands clear of the blade or cutter path, keep guards in place, use a push stick or featherboard where fitted, disconnect power before changing a blade or bit, and never defeat a guard or reach over a spinning blade.

demo.code:
SEQ=[100, 150, 220]
print('Grit progression: ' + ', '.join(str(x) for x in SEQ))
asc=all(SEQ[i]<SEQ[i+1] for i in range(len(SEQ)-1))
print('Steps: ' + str(len(SEQ)))
print('Strictly ascending: ' + str(asc))
print('First grit: ' + str(SEQ[0]) + ', last grit: ' + str(SEQ[-1]))
demo.expected_output:
Grit progression: 100, 150, 220
Steps: 3
Strictly ascending: True
First grit: 100, last grit: 220

title: Belt Sander
description: The belt sander removes material fast with a continuous abrasive belt, which makes it ideal for leveling glued-up panels and removing old finish, and dangerous for thin stock because it can gouge in a second. Keep the sander moving at all times, work with the grain, and start with 80-grit before moving to 120-grit. This guide covers leveling a glued-up pine panel, the classic belt-sander job. Clamp the panel, keep the cord clear, wear a dust mask, and never set the running sander down on the work.

image.description: Original diagram for Belt Sander: Glued-up pine panel leveled flat. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.

specs.tolerances: Panel flat within 1/32 inch across the width; no gouges deeper than 0.010 inch

Check flatness with a straightedge and repeat until the joints are flush.

Finish with the orbital sander at 150-grit before finishing.

title: Biscuit Joiner
description: The biscuit joiner cuts crescent-shaped slots in mating edges, and compressed beech biscuits swell with glue to align and reinforce panel joints. It is a fast alignment tool for tabletops and carcases, though it adds less strength than a mortise-and-tenon joint. This guide covers joining two pine boards edge-to-edge into a wider panel with size 20 biscuits. Mark both faces clearly so slots line up, keep the fence flat on the face, and let the glue cure fully before planing the panel.

title: Nail Gun
description: The pneumatic brad nailer drives small nails without hammer marks, which makes it ideal for trim and light assembly, but it is still a tool that fires a projectile, and it demands the same respect as any nail gun. Always keep the nose pressed to the work before firing, never point it at anyone, disconnect the air supply before clearing a jam, and wear eye protection. This guide covers nailing pine trim to a shelf unit with 1-1/4-inch brads, including setting the depth so nail heads sit just below the surface. Test depth on an offcut before firing into the finished piece.

title: Oscillating Multi-Tool
description: The oscillating multi-tool vibrates a small blade back and forth through a tiny arc, which lets it cut flush against a surface, plunge into a wall panel, or trim a door jamb in place, jobs no other saw can do. Blade choice is everything: wood blades for trim, bi-metal blades for nails, and a scraper blade for old adhesive. This guide covers trimming a pine door jamb flush to a new floor, a common repair job. Keep the blade flat, work slowly, and wear eye protection, because the tool throws fine dust and small chips.

title: Rotary Tool
description: The rotary tool is a small high-speed handpiece that takes tiny bits for carving, engraving, sanding, and polishing, and it is the right tool for detail work that larger tools cannot reach. Speeds run from 5,000 to 35,000 revolutions per minute, and small bits need high speeds while larger sanding drums need lower speeds. This guide covers engraving a simple maker's mark on a pine shelf end, a first rotary-tool project. Hold the tool like a pencil, brace your hands, wear eye protection, and never force a bit, because a stalled bit can snap.

image.description: Original diagram for Rotary Tool: Maker's mark engraved on a pine shelf end. The diagram shows the tool, blade, and work table with its key dimensions and features depicted.

details: Speed for engraving pine: about 20,000 rpm
specs.tolerances: Engraved lines even in depth within 1/64 inch; mark legible at arm's length

steps: Pencil the maker's mark on the pine shelf end and clamp the shelf to the bench.
Fit the 1/8-inch engraving bit and set the speed to 20,000 rpm.
Put on eye protection and practice the mark on an offcut first.
Trace the pencil lines with light, steady passes, letting the bit cut.
Brush away dust and deepen any faint lines with a second pass.
Seal the engraving with a dab of finish so it stays readable.

required: Rotary Tool (the tool of this guide)
Push stick or featherboard where applicable
tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection and hearing protection. Keep hands clear of the blade or cutter path, keep guards in place, use a push stick or featherboard where fitted, disconnect power before changing a blade or bit, and never defeat a guard or reach over a spinning blade.

title: Track Saw
description: The track saw runs along a guide rail that is clamped or gripped to the sheet, and it gives table-saw-straight cuts anywhere, including on full plywood sheets that are awkward to move. The rail's rubber splinter guard marks the exact cut line, so setup is a matter of aligning the guard with the mark. This guide covers cutting a plywood cabinet side square and straight with a track saw, the cleanest way to break down sheet goods on site. Check the blade depth, keep the cord behind the saw, and support the sheet so the offcut cannot drop and pinch.

specs.dimensions: 6-1/2-inch blade, plunge depth 2-1/8 inches, guide rail lengths 55 inches and 118 inches, bevel 0 to 47 degrees
details: Rail: 55 in standard, joins to 118 in
Cut straightness: within 0.004 in per foot on a true rail
fasteners: Cabinet side joined later with screws and glue
specs.tolerances: Cut straight within 1/64 inch over 48 inches; squareness within 1/64 inch over 24 inches
specs.arithmetic_note: Sheet yield checks out: floor of sheet width over piece width times floor of sheet height over piece height. Demo output below was captured by executing the demo code at build time.

steps: Support the plywood sheet flat and mark the cabinet-side cut line.
Lay the guide rail with its splinter guard exactly on the line and grip it to the sheet.
Set the blade depth to about 1/4 inch below the sheet and the bevel to 0 degrees.
Start the saw clear of the sheet, plunge, and push steadily along the rail.
Let the blade stop before lifting the saw, then check the cut edge for squareness.
Repeat for the matching cabinet side and compare the pair.

required: Track Saw (the tool of this guide)
Push stick or featherboard where applicable
tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection and hearing protection. Keep hands clear of the blade or cutter path, keep guards in place, use a push stick or featherboard where fitted, disconnect power before changing a blade or bit, and never defeat a guard or reach over a spinning blade.

SW=96
SH=48
PW=24
PH=30
across=int(SW//PW)
down=int(SH//PH)
tot=across*down
print('Sheet: ' + str(SW) + ' in x ' + str(SH) + ' in, piece: ' + str(PW) + ' in x ' + str(PH) + ' in')
print('Pieces across: ' + str(across) + ', pieces down: ' + str(down))
print('Pieces per sheet: ' + str(tot))
